justification: Human genetic evidence exists: Choi et al. (AJHG 2019) reported biallelic ADAMTS9 variants in families with nephronophthisis-related ciliopathy, with supporting functional work showing impaired ciliogenesis in patient-derived and knockdown cells. This is a direct, credible human gene–ciliopathy association, but the number of independent probands/families is small and independent replication has been limited, which argues against full "Established" status. Strong complementary biology exists in model systems: Nandadasa et al. (Nat Commun 2019) showed ADAMTS9/ADAMTS20 act non-canonically in ciliary vesicle growth and ciliogenesis, and Adamts9 mouse mutants show ciliopathy-like features (e.g., cardiac, renal, limb anomalies). Therefore most weight sits in Existing with substantial weight on Established, and residual weight on Hypothesized reflecting the strong animal/cell-based component of the evidence base.

SPG43 (OMIM 615043) was defined in a consanguineous Malian family with autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia, and exome sequencing by Landouré et al. (2013) identified a homozygous C19orf12 missense variant (p.Ala63Pro) segregating with disease, with an additional unrelated Brazilian patient carrying a C19orf12 variant. C19orf12 is also the established gene for MPAN/NBIA4, a mitochondrial membrane protein-associated neurodegeneration in which spastic paraparesis/corticospinal tract involvement is a core feature, and several subsequent cohorts have reported C19orf12 biallelic variants presenting as complicated or pure hereditary spastic paraplegia. Thus the gene–disease link is accepted and curated (OMIM/ClinGen-type assignment), though the number of families with the strict "SPG43" label is modest, leaving some weight for "Existing."

DIAPH3 is the gene underlying AUNA1 (autosomal dominant nonsyndromic auditory neuropathy 1, OMIM 609129), identified in a large North American family mapped to 13q14-21 and shown to carry a 5'UTR variant (c.-172G>A) causing DIAPH3 overexpression. This is strong human genetic evidence (linkage plus segregation plus expression data), but it derives essentially from a single large kindred, with replication largely coming from functional models (Drosophila dia overexpression and a transgenic DIAPH3-overexpressing mouse with auditory neuropathy-like phenotype and stereocilia defects) rather than independent probands. Thus the gene–disease relationship is widely regarded as causal and is the defining gene for this phenotype, yet independent human replication is sparse, justifying a split between Established and Existing. Supporting animal-model data add to the biological plausibility but cannot by themselves raise the classification.

IRAG1 (formerly MRVI1) encodes the IP3 receptor–associated cGMP kinase substrate that mediates NO/cGMP-dependent relaxation of gastrointestinal smooth muscle, the very pathway whose failure (loss of nitrergic inhibitory neurons/NO–cGMP signaling in the lower esophageal sphincter) defines achalasia; Irag-deficient mice show impaired NO-mediated smooth-muscle relaxation and gastric outlet/pyloric obstruction, giving strong biological plausibility. However, I am not aware of any human genetic study (GWAS or candidate-gene) reporting IRAG1/MRVI1 variants in idiopathic achalasia; the published achalasia genetics is dominated by HLA-DQ (Gockel et al. 2014) and candidate loci such as NOS1, VIPR1 and IL23R. Human variant evidence for MRVI1 exists mainly for infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, a distinct nitrergic smooth-muscle motility disorder that is related mechanistically but is not a recognized precursor or subtype of achalasia, so only limited points go to "Existing". The weight therefore falls on "Hypothesized" (pathway/animal-model evidence), with a residual probability that the association is essentially unexamined ("Novel") and almost none for "Established".

LAS1L is an X-linked gene (Xq12) encoding a component of the PELP1–TEX10–WDR18 ribosome biogenesis (pre-rRNA ITS2 processing) complex, and hemizygous missense variants have been reported in humans with X-linked neurodevelopmental phenotypes, including a family with a Wilson–Turner-like syndromic intellectual disability phenotype and a separate family with congenital lethal X-linked motor neuron disease showing a defect in ribosome biogenesis. The evidence rests on a small number of families and candidate variants from X-exome sequencing studies, with limited independent replication and some phenotypic heterogeneity, so the relationship is generally curated as limited/moderate rather than definitive. Functional data (ribosome biogenesis, rRNA processing defects, neural expression) provide a plausible mechanism, supporting at least a hypothesized basis if the human genetic reports are discounted. I therefore concentrate points on "Existing," with a modest allocation to "Established" and a meaningful reserve for "Hypothesized."

PDGFRA has very strong developmental-biology support for a role in cardiac morphogenesis: the mouse Patch (Pdgfra-null) mutant and conditional/neural-crest and epicardial deletions produce outflow tract septation defects, conotruncal anomalies, coronary vascular and valve abnormalities, placing it firmly in the Hypothesized tier on mechanism alone. Human genetic evidence is sparse: I recall candidate-gene/gene–environment analyses (e.g., PDGFRA polymorphisms with maternal binge drinking and obstructive heart defects, using National Birth Defects Prevention Study-type data) and PDGFRA promoter haplotype work in neural tube defects, but no replicated, definitive demonstration that PDGFRA variants cause congenital heart disease in humans. PDGFRA is not listed as a Mendelian CHD gene in clinical gene panels or ClinGen curations; germline/somatic PDGFRA variation is instead classically linked to GIST and hypereosinophilic syndrome. Therefore most weight goes to Hypothesized, with a moderate share to Existing for the limited human association reports, and only minimal weight to Established.

SHANK3 is the designated gene for OMIM "schizophrenia 15" (SCZD15, 22q13.33), based primarily on Gauthier et al. (2010), who identified two de novo SHANK3 mutations (R1117X and R536W) in unrelated families ascertained for schizophrenia, with functional consequences on synaptic protein localization. Additional human support comes from case series of 22q13.3 deletion/Phelan-McDermid syndrome patients presenting with psychotic or bipolar/schizoaffective phenotypes, and from rare SHANK3 variants in broader neurodevelopmental/psychiatric cohorts, though SHANK3 is far better established for autism and intellectual disability than for schizophrenia specifically. Because the schizophrenia-specific genetic evidence rests largely on a small number of de novo variants and case reports without robust large-scale replication (SHANK3 is not a genome-wide significant schizophrenia gene in large sequencing studies such as SCHEMA), the evidence is credible but not definitive. Abundant biological and mouse-model data (synaptic scaffolding, glutamatergic/NMDA signaling, Shank3-deficient mice with social and sensorimotor gating deficits) support a plausible mechanism, justifying residual weight on Hypothesized.

SLC34A1 encodes the renal proximal tubule sodium-phosphate cotransporter NaPi-IIa, and biallelic loss-of-function was reported by Magen et al. (NEJM 2010) in a consanguineous family with renal Fanconi syndrome and hypophosphatemic rickets, which is the basis for the OMIM entry FRTS2 (#613388). However, that evidence rests largely on a single family, and subsequent work showed that recessive SLC34A1 mutations more consistently produce idiopathic infantile hypercalcemia type 2 with hypophosphatemia, nephrocalcinosis and often only partial/incomplete proximal tubulopathy, so the specific "Fanconi renotubular syndrome 2" designation is considered by some curators as limited or disputed rather than firmly replicated. Heterozygous variants have also been linked to hypophosphatemia and nephrolithiasis (Prié et al. 2002), though this too has been questioned. The gene's biology (proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption, Slc34a1 knockout mice with hypophosphatemia and hypercalciuria) strongly supports plausibility. I therefore weight Existing highest, with meaningful probability for Established.

phenotype: intellectual disability, anterior maxillary protrusion, and strabismus
justification: SOBP (also called JXC1) is the gene underlying autosomal recessive "mental retardation, anterior maxillary protrusion, and strabismus" (MRAMS syndrome, OMIM 613671), established by Birk et al. (2010), who identified a homozygous nonsense mutation segregating in a large consanguineous Israeli Arab kindred and also reported an SOBP variant in a family with nonsyndromic intellectual disability. The gene is highly expressed in the developing brain limbic system, and the mouse Sobp mutant (jackson circler) shows inner ear and neurodevelopmental defects, providing supportive biological plausibility. Additional probands with biallelic SOBP variants have since been reported in consanguineous ID cohorts, but the total number of independent families remains small, so curation efforts generally rate the gene–disease relationship as moderate rather than definitive. I therefore split the weight mainly between Established and Existing, with a small residual for Hypothesized reflecting the heavy reliance on animal/expression data for mechanism.

SPTAN1 is firmly established for de novo (in-frame) variants causing developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, and dominant nonsense variants causing juvenile-onset distal hereditary motor neuropathy, a phenotype that frequently overlaps with spastic paraplegia/pyramidal signs. For hereditary spastic paraplegia specifically, there is at least one credible human genetic report describing biallelic SPTAN1 variants in families with autosomal recessive HSP, plus occasional candidate findings in HSP/complex spastic-ataxia gene-panel and exome cohorts, but the number of independent probands is small and segregation/functional support is limited, so curation bodies classify the gene–HSP relationship as limited rather than definitive. The biology is highly supportive: αII-spectrin is a core component of the periodic axonal membrane skeleton of long corticospinal axons, and spectrin/cytoskeletal genes (e.g., SPTBN2, SPAST, KIF1A) are classic motor-axon degeneration genes, with animal/cell models showing axonal degeneration upon αII-spectrin loss. Hence most weight goes to "Existing," with meaningful residual probability on "Hypothesized" (if the human HSP reports are considered too sparse) and a smaller share on "Established."

Cowden syndrome 6 (OMIM 615109) is designated in OMIM as caused by germline AKT1 mutation, based principally on Orloff et al. (2013, Am J Hum Genet), who identified germline AKT1 p.Glu17Lys (and related variants) in a small fraction (~0.6%) of PTEN-mutation–negative Cowden/Cowden-like probands, with functional evidence of AKT pathway hyperactivation in patient lymphoblastoid/tissue samples. This is human genetic evidence in multiple unrelated probands from a single large cohort, but independent replication has been sparse and subsequent ClinGen-style curations of AKT1 for Cowden syndrome have tended toward limited validity, since the recurrent E17K variant is more firmly linked to mosaic Proteus syndrome and somatic cancers. Strong supporting biology exists (AKT1 is directly downstream of PTEN/PI3K, the canonical Cowden pathway), which would justify at least a hypothesized relationship even absent the genetic data. I therefore split points mainly between Existing and Established, with a small residual for Hypothesized.

ARL14EP (also known as C11orf46) lies within the 11p13–p14 WAGR deletion interval, and its haploinsufficiency has been proposed to contribute to the corpus callosum abnormalities and neurodevelopmental features seen in some WAGR syndrome patients — evidence that is suggestive but confounded by the contiguous-gene nature of the deletion. The strongest mechanistic data come from Akbarian/Jiang-lab work showing that C11orf46/ARL14EP acts as a chromatin/transcriptional regulator (repressing Sema6a and related axon-guidance genes) and that its knockdown in mouse cortex disrupts callosal axon projections, which is animal/in vitro evidence and therefore supports "Hypothesized." I am not aware of replicated, independent human families with pathogenic point variants in ARL14EP causing a Mendelian neurodevelopmental disorder, so "Established" receives few points; candidate-gene listings in consanguineous intellectual disability cohorts, if present, would only support limited human evidence. Thus the bulk of probability falls on Hypothesized with a substantial minority on Existing.

CNKSR1 encodes a multidomain scaffold (CNK1) for Ras/Rho/MAPK signaling, and its paralog CNKSR2 is a well-established X-linked intellectual disability/epilepsy-aphasia (Houge syndrome) gene, giving strong pathway and family-level biological plausibility for a role in neurodevelopment. However, I am not aware of replicated human genetic studies implicating CNKSR1 variants in intellectual disability, autism, or related neurodevelopmental phenotypes; most CNKSR1-specific literature concerns Ras/ERK signaling, insulin signaling, and cancer (e.g., pancreatic cancer invasion). CNKSR1 at 1p36.11 lies outside the classical 1p36 deletion critical regions, so contiguous-gene deletion evidence is weak. Points are therefore concentrated on Hypothesized (pathway/paralog/expression-based plausibility) with a modest allowance for isolated case reports or candidate-gene mentions in exome/NDD cohorts that I may not recall, and a substantial Novel allocation reflecting the real possibility that no credible human evidence exists.

COQ5 encodes a C-methyltransferase in the coenzyme Q10 biosynthesis pathway, a pathway in which biallelic defects (COQ2, COQ4, COQ8A, PDSS1/2, etc.) are well-established causes of primary CoQ10 deficiency with encephalopathy, developmental delay, and cerebellar ataxia. For COQ5 specifically, the principal human genetic evidence is a single consanguineous family (three affected siblings) with cerebellar ataxia, intellectual disability and static encephalomyopathy attributed to a homozygous 3'UTR duplication reducing COQ5 protein, with supportive biochemical and yeast complementation data. Because this rests largely on one family with few, if any, independently replicated probands, the evidence is credible but not definitive, favoring "Existing" over "Established." Strong pathway biology, yeast coq5 mutant data, and the broader CoQ10 deficiency phenotype spectrum provide additional non-genetic (hypothesized-level) support, and there is essentially no basis for "Novel."

CRYGB is the gene assigned to OMIM "Cataract 39, multiple types" (CTRCT39), and the gene encodes gamma-B crystallin, a major structural lens protein whose destabilization is a well-established mechanism of congenital/early-onset cataract. The principal human evidence is a small number of reports, notably an autosomal dominant congenital cataract family (Kuwaiti) with CRYGB variants, plus scattered additional variant reports in Chinese/other cataract cohorts; replication across many independent probands is limited, and some curation efforts consider the gene–disease evidence limited. Strong supporting biology exists from mouse Cryg cluster mutants (including Crygb) producing nuclear/lens opacities and from in vitro protein-stability/aggregation studies, which would support at least a Hypothesized rating even if human data were discounted. Therefore most weight goes to Existing, with meaningful probability of Established and residual weight on Hypothesized.

H3-4 (formerly HIST3H3) encodes the testis-enriched histone H3.4/H3.1t variant, and I am not aware of any replicated human genetic study reporting de novo or inherited pathogenic H3-4 variants in neurodevelopmental disorder. The well-established "chromatinopathy" histone genes in NDD are H3-3A/H3-3B (Bryant–Li–Bhoj syndrome), H1-4 (Rahman syndrome), and several H4 cluster genes (H4C3, H4C5, H4C9, H4C11), which are frequently confused with H3-4 because of the new HGNC histone nomenclature. Strong biological plausibility nonetheless exists: H3-4 is a canonical core histone H3 paralog, and missense changes at homologous residues in other H3 genes disrupt nucleosome function, chromatin regulation, and neurodevelopment, so a pathway/paralog-based hypothesis is reasonable. A small residual probability is retained for isolated case reports or cohort-level variant findings (e.g., in large DDD/exome NDD cohorts) that I may not recall, which would justify "Existing". Overall the evidence base is predominantly indirect/biological rather than variant-level human genetic.

OMIM designates NARCOLEPSY 7 (NRCLP7, 614250) on the basis of a missense variant (p.Ser133Cys) in MOG, located at 6p22.1 near the HLA region, identified by Hor et al. (2011, Am J Hum Genet) in a multiplex family with narcolepsy–cataplexy; functional work showed abnormal protein aggregation/trafficking of the mutant MOG. This is a credible human genetic study and is the defining evidence for the phenotype designation, which supports "Existing." However, the evidence rests essentially on a single family with limited independent replication in other probands or cohorts, so full "Established" status is not warranted. Additional supportive but indirect human biology (MOG as an oligodendrocyte autoantigen, autoimmune hypothesis of hypocretin neuron loss, HLA-linked chromosomal position) underpins the smaller "Hypothesized" allocation; a "Novel" rating is essentially excluded because the gene–phenotype pair is the basis of the OMIM entry itself.

MYBPC3 is unequivocally established for hypertrophic (and some dilated/restrictive) cardiomyopathy, but these are myocardial diseases rather than structural congenital heart disease (CHD). Human evidence linking MYBPC3 to CHD proper is limited: sarcomere genes (chiefly MYH7, MYH6, ACTC1) dominate associations with left ventricular non-compaction, atrial septal defect and Ebstein anomaly, while MYBPC3 appears sporadically in LVNC cohorts and in large CHD exome/de novo sequencing studies without statistical or replicated proband-level support. Because LVNC and biallelic neonatal MYBPC3 cardiomyopathy are sometimes classified within the congenital cardiac spectrum, a moderate "Existing" weight is warranted. Strong myocardial/sarcomere biology and mouse models of cardiac development give substantial weight to "Hypothesized," while the absence of replicated causal data for septal, conotruncal or valvular malformations keeps "Established" low and leaves some probability for "Novel."

NDUFA12 encodes an accessory subunit of mitochondrial complex I, and biallelic loss-of-function variants have been reported in human patients with isolated complex I deficiency presenting as Leigh/Leigh-like syndrome (OMIM: mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 23). The number of independent probands is relatively small (a handful of families reported since ~2017–2021), with functional support from patient fibroblasts/muscle showing reduced complex I assembly and activity rescued by wild-type cDNA, so the evidence is credible and partly replicated but not as extensive as for core Leigh genes such as SURF1 or NDUFS4. There is also historical confusion with NDUFAF2 (formerly NDUFA12L/B17.2L), an established Leigh syndrome gene, which inflates perceived evidence for NDUFA12 itself. I therefore split points mainly between Established and Existing, with a small residual for Hypothesized given the strong pathway/biological rationale.

PECR encodes peroxisomal trans-2-enoyl-CoA reductase, an enzyme of peroxisomal fatty acid elongation; because peroxisomal fatty acid metabolism defects (e.g., Zellweger spectrum, D-bifunctional protein deficiency) classically produce neurodevelopmental impairment, there is a plausible biological/pathway rationale, which supports a substantial Hypothesized weight. I am not aware of robust, replicated human genetic studies demonstrating that PECR variants cause intellectual disability, autism, or another neurodevelopmental disorder, so Established is very unlikely. The best-known human genetic signals at PECR come from alcohol dependence GWAS/linkage work (Treutlein et al., 2009) and other metabolic/lipid traits, which are not clearly neurodevelopmental, so only limited points go to Existing in case isolated case reports or candidate-gene findings in developmental delay cohorts exist that I cannot recall with confidence. A meaningful share remains on Novel because PECR is not present on standard neurodevelopmental gene panels and has no ClinGen/OMIM-recognized NDD disease entry.

PRICKLE2 encodes a non-canonical Wnt/planar cell polarity protein that interacts with synaptic proteins (including PSD-95 and components shared with PRICKLE1/SYNAPSIN I pathways), and Prickle2-deficient mice show autism-like behaviors and reduced synaptic connectivity, which supports at least a hypothesized role. Human evidence exists: rare missense variants (e.g., E8Q, V153I) were reported in individuals with autism spectrum disorder, and PRICKLE2 variants have been implicated in seizure phenotypes alongside PRICKLE1 (progressive myoclonic epilepsy), with 3p14.1 deletions encompassing PRICKLE2 described in patients with developmental delay, epilepsy and ASD features. However, these reports involve small numbers of probands, limited segregation data, and incomplete replication in large sequencing cohorts, so causality for a broad complex neurodevelopmental disorder is suggestive rather than definitive. SFARI-type curation treats PRICKLE2 as a suggestive/moderate-evidence candidate rather than an established gene. Hence most weight goes to "Existing," with a meaningful share retained for "Hypothesized" because much of the mechanistic support is from mouse and in vitro work.

SEPTIN12 (SEPT12) is the gene assigned to OMIM "spermatogenic failure 10" (SPGF10) on the basis of human sequencing studies, principally Kuo et al. (Hum Mutat 2012), which reported heterozygous missense variants (e.g., T89M, D197N) in infertile men with oligozoospermia/teratozoospermia and defective sperm annulus, supported by functional assays showing impaired filament formation. Supporting biology is strong: SEPT12 is testis-specific, localizes to the sperm annulus, and Sept12 mutant/chimeric mice show spermiogenesis defects, bent tails and nuclear damage. However, the human genetic evidence remains limited — few independent probands, mostly heterozygous missense alleles of uncertain penetrance, and limited independent replication — so many curation efforts would rate this as limited rather than definitive. I therefore weight "Existing" highest, with meaningful probability for "Established" given the OMIM phenotype designation and some additional reports, and residual weight on "Hypothesized" reflecting the possibility that most support is animal/in vitro.

TECR (trans-2,3-enoyl-CoA reductase, GPSN2) is listed in OMIM as the gene for autosomal recessive non-syndromic intellectual disability type 14 (MRT14), based essentially on a single homozygous missense variant (p.Pro182Leu) identified by homozygosity mapping and exome sequencing in a consanguineous Hutterite kindred (Çalışkan et al., 2011). Independent replication in additional unrelated families has been scarce, and gene–disease validity curation has generally regarded the evidence as limited rather than definitive. Supporting biology exists: TECR catalyzes the final reduction step of very-long-chain fatty acid elongation, a pathway in which several genes (ELOVL4, HACD1, CERS1) are linked to neurodevelopmental/neurological disease, and TECR is highly expressed in brain. Therefore most weight goes to "Existing," with a modest allowance for "Established" (OMIM-recognized MRT gene) and for "Hypothesized" (pathway/functional support without robust replicated human genetic proof).

TRIM69 is a well-characterized interferon-stimulated gene with direct antiviral activity: it restricts vesicular stomatitis virus transcription, inhibits dengue virus by ubiquitinating/degrading NS3, and has been implicated in restriction of other RNA viruses, making a biological link to host antiviral defense strong. However, this evidence comes from in vitro work in human and other cell lines, overexpression/knockdown studies, and virology experiments rather than from patients with inherited susceptibility to infection. I am not aware of any replicated human genetic study (Mendelian or robust association/GWAS) linking rare or common TRIM69 variants to primary immunodeficiency or hereditary predisposition to infection, nor of TRIM69 appearing on inborn-errors-of-immunity gene panels. Accordingly, the bulk of the weight belongs in Hypothesized, with a small allowance for an unrecalled candidate-gene polymorphism association (Existing) and for the possibility that no credible link exists (Novel).

ZBTB40 is best known from genome-wide association and sequencing studies of bone mineral density, osteoporosis and osteogenesis imperfecta-like phenotypes, not neurodevelopmental disease. I am not aware of any replicated human genetic study implicating ZBTB40 variants in intellectual disability, autism, or developmental delay; it is not on established NDD gene panels or ClinGen/SFARI high-confidence lists. Some plausibility exists because other BTB–zinc-finger transcription factors (ZBTB18, ZBTB20, ZBTB11) are bona fide ID genes and ZBTB40 lies in the broader 1p36 region frequently deleted in patients with developmental delay, which could generate incidental co-mentions or hypothesis-level claims. Occasional appearance of ZBTB40 as a candidate de novo variant in large exome cohorts cannot be excluded, so a small amount of weight is placed on "Existing." Overall the evidence base is dominated by skeletal phenotypes, leaving the NDD link largely novel/speculative.

The ABCB6–ocular coloboma/microphthalmia link rests chiefly on a single key human genetic report (Wang et al., AJHG 2012), which identified heterozygous ABCB6 missense variants segregating in families with isolated coloboma and some sporadic cases, supported by zebrafish abcb6 knockdown producing eye/coloboma-like defects. This led to the OMIM designation MCOPCB7, but independent replication in additional unrelated probands has been sparse, and ABCB6 is better established for dyschromatosis universalis hereditaria, familial pseudohyperkalemia, and the Lan blood group, where many variants (including nulls) are not associated with eye malformations — raising questions about causality and penetrance. Therefore human genetic evidence exists but is limited rather than firmly replicated, favoring "Existing" with some weight on "Established" given the original multi-family segregation and functional data.

AP2A2 encodes an alpha subunit of the AP-2 adaptor complex central to clathrin-mediated endocytosis and synaptic vesicle recycling, a process repeatedly implicated in schizophrenia pathophysiology (synaptic/endocytic gene sets are enriched in schizophrenia rare-variant and pathway analyses), which provides a plausible biological rationale (Hypothesized). However, I am not aware of any replicated, gene-specific human genetic study demonstrating that AP2A2 variants cause schizophrenia, and AP2A2 is not among the genome-wide significant prioritized genes commonly reported in PGC schizophrenia GWAS or SCHEMA exome results. Any mention of AP2A2 in schizophrenia literature is most likely as part of broader endocytosis/synaptic pathway enrichment or proteomic surveys rather than direct variant-level association. Therefore the weight falls on Hypothesized/Novel, with a small allowance for an isolated association or inclusion in a candidate pathway-based human study that I may not recall. Established evidence is essentially absent.

phenotype: hemolytic uremic syndrome, atypical, susceptibility to, 1
justification: The common deletion of the CFHR3–CFHR1 region is one of the best-replicated genetic susceptibility factors for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, reported in multiple independent human cohorts (German, French, Spanish, UK, Indian) and strongly associated with the anti-complement factor H autoantibody subtype of aHUS (DEAP-HUS). Functional work supports a mechanism in which loss of CFHR1/CFHR3 permits autoantibody generation against the C-terminal recognition domain of factor H, impairing complement regulation on endothelial surfaces. Points are distributed mainly to Established because of replicated human genetic association across populations, with some weight on Existing because the deletion acts as a susceptibility/modifier allele rather than a fully penetrant monogenic cause, and because the CFHR3 deletion is usually inseparable from CFHR1 deletion, complicating gene-level attribution. Minimal weight is left for Hypothesized/Novel given the abundance of direct human genetic evidence.

CPA6 is the gene assigned to OMIM "epilepsy, familial temporal lobe, 5" (ETL5) based primarily on a single key human genetics study (Salzmann et al., Hum Mutat 2012) that identified a homozygous CPA6 mutation in a consanguineous family with febrile seizures/temporal lobe epilepsy plus heterozygous rare variants in sporadic TLE patients, with supporting in vitro enzymatic loss-of-function data. Additional human reports (e.g., Sapio et al. 2015) described CPA6 variants in febrile seizures and juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, broadening but not firmly replicating the TLE-specific association. Evidence remains limited: few independent families, incomplete segregation, and relatively frequent rare CPA6 missense variants in population databases have led curation efforts to regard the gene–disease relationship as limited/disputed rather than definitive. CPA6 biology (extracellular matrix metallocarboxypeptidase processing neuropeptides in brain) provides a plausible mechanism, supporting some weight on Hypothesized, but the core evidence is human genetic, so most points go to Existing.

CTNNA3 encodes αT-catenin, an area composita protein that interacts with plakophilin-2 at the cardiac intercalated disc, making it a strong biological candidate for arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC). Human genetic evidence comes principally from van Hengel et al. (2013), who identified two rare variants (p.V94D and c.281delA) in ARVC probands from a mutation-negative cohort, with in vitro functional data suggesting impaired dimerization and altered binding to plakophilin-2; a few subsequent case reports/cohorts have reported additional rare CTNNA3 variants. However, replication has been sparse, segregation data are weak, and the ClinGen ARVC gene curation expert panel classified CTNNA3 as having only "Limited" evidence for ARVC, so causality is not firmly established. Supporting animal data (Ctnna3-null mice developing dilated cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia-prone remodeling) bolster the biological plausibility but are non-human. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing," with residual weight on "Hypothesized" and a small amount on "Established."

FOXD3 is a well-characterized forkhead transcription factor required for neural crest specification and maintenance, and the periocular neural crest gives rise to the corneal endothelium/stroma, iris stroma and trabecular meshwork — tissues whose maldevelopment produces anterior segment dysgenesis (Axenfeld–Rieger spectrum, Peters anomaly). Zebrafish foxd3 (sym1/mother superior) mutants and conditional Foxd3 mouse knockouts show neural crest deficits with craniofacial and ocular consequences, providing a plausible biological, animal-model-based link. However, I am not aware of any human genetic study reporting FOXD3 variants in probands or families with anterior segment dysgenesis; the established human ASD genes remain PITX2, FOXC1, FOXE3, PAX6, CYP1B1, PXDN and others, and the only notable human FOXD3 variant literature concerns a promoter variant in familial vitiligo. Accordingly most weight goes to Hypothesized, with a substantial residual for Novel because the gene–phenotype pairing may be purely inferential, and only minimal weight to Existing/Established.

FUS is the gene assigned to OMIM "tremor, hereditary essential, 4 (ETM4)" based on a single exome-sequencing study of a large French-Canadian family in which a nonsense variant (p.Gln290*) segregated with essential tremor, plus two additional rare missense variants in screening cohorts (Merner et al., 2012). However, multiple independent replication efforts in European, North American and Asian ET cohorts failed to identify pathogenic FUS variants, and subsequent reports (e.g., FUS p.Arg377Trp in a family) have been inconsistent, leading curation efforts to regard the gene–disease relationship as limited or disputed rather than definitive. Therefore the human genetic evidence is credible but not replicated robustly, placing most weight on "Existing" with only modest weight on "Established". Supporting biology (FUS as an RNA-binding protein implicated in ALS/FTD neurodegeneration, with cerebellar/Purkinje cell relevance to tremor circuits) justifies some "Hypothesized" weight, and the small residual probability reflects the possibility that the association is spurious.

KCTD13 lies within the 16p11.2 BP4–BP5 CNV interval, one of the most robustly replicated genomic risk loci for autism, intellectual disability, and head-size abnormalities, and a few human reports describe smaller atypical deletions narrowing the critical region to KCTD13/ASPHD1/SEZ6L2 — providing suggestive but gene-nonspecific human genetic support. The strongest claim that KCTD13 is the "major driver" of the 16p11.2 head-size phenotype comes from zebrafish overexpression/knockdown work (Golzio et al. 2012) and subsequent mouse models (Escamilla et al. 2017; Arbogast et al. 2019), which are animal rather than human genetic evidence and gave partly conflicting results. Protein-network analyses implicate a KCTD13–CUL3–RhoA pathway in cortical mid-fetal development, again biological rather than variant-based. To date there is no replicated set of independent probands with pathogenic single-gene KCTD13 point variants causing a Mendelian neurodevelopmental disorder, so "Established" is unlikely; most weight belongs to Hypothesized with substantial Existing credit for the CNV/narrowed-deletion human data.

RNLS (renalase) is a secreted FAD-dependent amine oxidase/cytokine studied mainly in the context of blood pressure regulation, catecholamine metabolism, chronic kidney disease, cardiac ischemia, and type 1 diabetes susceptibility (rs10509540). I am not aware of any human genetic study—linkage, candidate-gene, or GWAS—reporting variants in RNLS as a cause of or association with congenital or age-related cataract, nor of a Mendelian cataract gene at this locus (the nearest well-known lens gene on 10q is PITX3, which is distinct and distant). Indirect, weak support could be argued because RNLS variation is associated with diabetes and oxidative/mitochondrial stress pathways, and diabetes is a recognized risk factor for cataract, which also leaves room for a hypothesized biological link via redox regulation in the lens. However, there is no direct lens expression or animal-model cataract evidence that I can recall, so the bulk of probability belongs to Novel with a meaningful share to Hypothesized.

SLC4A8 (NDCBE) encodes a neuronal Na+-driven Cl-/HCO3- exchanger that regulates intracellular pH and modulates presynaptic glutamate release and neuronal excitability, which provides a plausible biological link to glutamatergic/pH hypotheses of schizophrenia; mouse knockout data (Sinning et al.) support this mechanistic relevance, but such evidence is animal/in vitro and therefore maps to "Hypothesized." I am not aware of any replicated genome-wide significant schizophrenia association at SLC4A8, nor of well-powered candidate-gene or rare-variant studies implicating it in schizophrenia probands (note that the robust schizophrenia gene SLC39A8 is frequently confused with SLC4A8). A small possibility remains that SLC4A8 lies within a broader PGC schizophrenia locus or appeared in an underpowered association/expression study, so a modest weight is given to "Existing." "Established" is essentially excluded given the absence of replicated human causal evidence, while some weight to "Novel" reflects the possibility that all mentions are incidental or pertain to other phenotypes (hypertension, epilepsy).

TNIK was reported as a candidate gene for autosomal-recessive non-syndromic intellectual disability in large consanguineous-family homozygosity-mapping/exome studies (notably Najmabadi et al. 2011 and subsequent consanguineous ID cohorts), and it is listed in curated ID candidate-gene resources such as SysID, which supports at least "Existing" human genetic evidence. However, the number of independent probands/families with convincing biallelic or de novo TNIK variants is small and replication is limited, so full "Established" status (as in ClinGen-style definitive curation) is not clearly supported. Strong supporting biology exists: TNIK is a postsynaptic density kinase interacting with DISC1, NMDA-receptor complexes and Wnt signaling, and Tnik-knockout mice show cognitive impairment, which underpins a substantial "Hypothesized" weight. TNIK has also been implicated in schizophrenia-related association studies, a neuropsychiatric but not strictly ID phenotype. Overall, evidence is suggestive but not definitive for causation of non-syndromic ID.

ABCB6 is the recognized gene for autosomal dominant familial pseudohyperkalemia (PSHK2, OMIM 609153), a red-cell cation leak disorder. Missense variants in ABCB6 (e.g., p.Arg375Trp, p.Arg375Gln) were identified in several independent FP families (including FP-Lille, FP-Falkirk, FP-Chiswick/Edinburgh pedigrees) after linkage to 2q35, with co-segregation and recurrent mutational hotspots, and functional work supporting altered erythrocyte cation transport. ABCB6 variants also cause dyschromatosis universalis hereditaria and ocular coloboma, indicating allelic heterogeneity, and some reports note incomplete penetrance of the cation-leak phenotype, which leaves a small residual uncertainty. Overall the human genetic evidence is replicated across multiple probands/families, supporting "Established," with a modest allocation to "Existing" because the number of independent reports is relatively limited compared with other erythrocyte-membrane disease genes.

AGBL1 is the designated gene for Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy type 8 (FECD8, OMIM 615523) based primarily on a single key human genetic study (Riazuddin et al., AJHG 2013), which reported a nonsense variant segregating in a large late-onset FECD family plus additional rare missense variants in unrelated probands, with functional data showing altered interaction with TCF4 (the major FECD-associated transcription factor). This constitutes credible human genetic evidence, so the relationship is clearly more than hypothesized. However, independent replication has been sparse, and subsequent cohort screens (including in Chinese, Japanese and European populations) have not consistently confirmed a causal role, with some variants being too frequent in controls, leading several curation efforts to regard the evidence as limited/disputed. I therefore weight "Existing" most heavily, with meaningful but minority probability on "Established" given OMIM's formal gene–phenotype assignment.

CDK6 is the designated gene for MCPH12 (OMIM 616080) based primarily on a single consanguineous Pakistani family in which a homozygous missense variant (p.Ala197Thr) segregated with primary microcephaly, with supporting functional work showing CDK6 localizes to the centrosome and that the mutant protein mislocalizes and disrupts centrosome/spindle organization (Hussain et al., 2013). Replication in additional independent probands/families has been very limited, so the evidence falls short of the "multiple independent families" standard for Established and is best described as credible but not definitive human genetic evidence. Strong supporting biology (CDK6 role in neural progenitor proliferation, centrosomal localization, and shared pathway with other MCPH genes) adds plausibility but is mechanistic rather than additional genetic proof. Hence most weight to Existing, with some probability that newer case reports/ClinGen curation would elevate it to Established and some residual weight that the evidence is essentially one family plus functional data (Hypothesized).

Biallelic DDX59 variants were first identified by Shamseldin et al. (2013) in consanguineous families with orofaciodigital syndrome (OFD type V/Thurston-type), a disorder classified within the ciliopathy spectrum, and the authors also showed reduced GLI/hedgehog signaling consistent with a ciliary mechanism. Additional human reports (e.g., Salpietro et al.) described further probands with homozygous loss-of-function DDX59 variants presenting with OFD features plus neurological involvement, providing independent replication. OMIM lists DDX59 as the gene for orofaciodigital syndrome V, supporting a causal role. However, the total number of reported families is still small, DDX59 is an RNA helicase whose direct ciliary role is less well established than for canonical ciliopathy genes, and some curation efforts may consider the evidence moderate rather than definitive — hence a substantial share of weight on "Existing."

phenotype: fetal akinesia-cerebral and retinal hemorrhage syndrome
justification: The phenotype corresponds to lethal congenital contracture syndrome 5 (LCCS5, OMIM 615368), described in a consanguineous family with a homozygous DNM2 missense variant (p.Phe379Val) by Koutsopoulos et al. (2013), with affected fetuses showing akinesia, contractures, and cerebral/retinal hemorrhages. This is credible human genetic evidence with supporting functional studies (altered dynamin-2 oligomerization/GTPase activity), but replication in additional independent, unrelated probands is sparse, so the gene–disease relationship is generally curated as limited/moderate rather than definitive. DNM2 is unambiguously established for other allelic disorders (autosomal dominant centronuclear myopathy, CMT dominant-intermediate B), which strengthens biological plausibility for a severe recessive fetal phenotype. Accordingly most weight goes to "Existing," with some probability for "Established" given the specificity of the OMIM/Orphanet entity, and a small residual for "Hypothesized" if the single-family evidence is considered insufficient.

LCAT deficiency (familial LCAT deficiency and fish-eye disease) is a well-characterized Mendelian disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in the LCAT gene on 16q22; no other locus has been established as causal. DTHD1 (death domain containing 1, 4p14) is a poorly characterized gene reported mainly in the context of recurrent bacterial meningitis/immune susceptibility and sporadically in neurodevelopmental or cancer candidate-gene lists, with no known role in HDL metabolism, cholesterol esterification, or apolipoprotein biology. I am aware of no human genetic study, functional study, or animal model linking DTHD1 to LCAT activity or to the LCAT deficiency phenotype (corneal opacity, anemia, proteinuric renal disease, low HDL). A small residual probability is left for an incidental GWAS co-mention or an unreported modifier/digenic observation. Overall, this pair appears Novel.

ELMOD3 was first linked to nonsyndromic hearing loss through a large consanguineous Pakistani family mapping to DFNB88, in which a homozygous nonsense/missense variant segregated with prelingual severe-to-profound deafness (Jaworek et al., PLoS Genetics 2013). A subsequent Chinese family with autosomal dominant postlingual hearing loss (DFNA81) was reported with an ELMOD3 variant, providing a second independent human observation, and additional variants have appeared in deafness gene panel/exome cohorts. However, the total number of well-segregating independent families remains small and ClinGen-type curation of this gene for hearing loss has generally been at the limited/moderate rather than definitive level, so "Established" is not fully supported. Strong supporting biology exists—ELMOD3 is an ARL2 GTPase-activating protein expressed in hair cell stereocilia, and Elmod3-knockout mice show hearing loss with stereocilia abnormalities—but these are non-human data and only reinforce plausibility. I therefore weight most probability on Existing, with meaningful mass on Established.

phenotype: hypogonadotropic hypogonadism 21 with or without anosmia
justification: FLRT3 is the gene assigned to OMIM "hypogonadotropic hypogonadism 21 with or without anosmia" (HH21) on the basis of a single landmark human study (Miraoui et al., AJHG 2013), which identified rare heterozygous FLRT3 variants in patients with congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism/Kallmann syndrome as part of a screen of FGF8-signaling pathway genes; most variants were found in an oligogenic context with incomplete penetrance. Independent replication in additional unrelated probands has been very limited, and subsequent gene-curation efforts have tended to regard FLRT3 as having limited/questionable evidence for monogenic CHH. Supporting biology is strong: FLRT3 modulates FGF receptor signaling and is involved in neuronal/axonal guidance and cell adhesion, pathways central to GnRH neuron migration and olfactory bulb development. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing" (credible human genetic report, not definitive), with residual weight on "Established" (OMIM phenotype designation) and "Hypothesized" (pathway/functional data).

MAP2K2 (MEK2) is a definitively established disease gene within the RASopathy spectrum, but its principal, replicated human phenotype is cardio-facio-cutaneous (CFC) syndrome rather than classic Noonan syndrome. Human mutation studies (Rodriguez-Viciana 2006; Nava 2007; Dentici 2009; Schulz 2008) report patients with MAP2K2 variants whose phenotypes overlap with or were initially diagnosed as Noonan syndrome, and MAP2K2 is included on many Noonan/RASopathy diagnostic panels; CFC is a well-recognized Noonan-spectrum allelic/phenotypic neighbor caused by the same RAS–MAPK pathway activation. However, curated gene–disease validity assessments generally assign MAP2K2 to CFC rather than Noonan syndrome proper, so evidence for MAP2K2 specifically causing Noonan syndrome is limited and often reflects diagnostic overlap. Strong mechanistic support (gain-of-function MEK2 kinase activity, mouse and zebrafish RASopathy models) underpins the biological plausibility. Hence most weight goes to Existing, with meaningful weight to Established and some to Hypothesized.

MRPL12 encodes a mitochondrial large ribosomal subunit protein essential for mitochondrial translation, and loss of function plausibly produces a combined OXPHOS (multiple respiratory chain complex) deficiency, which is the basis for the COXPD45 designation. The principal human genetic evidence is a single consanguineous proband with a homozygous missense MRPL12 variant presenting with growth retardation, neurological deterioration, and reduced mitochondrial translation, with supporting functional studies in patient fibroblasts (Serre et al., 2013). To my knowledge, independent replication in additional unrelated probands is sparse or absent, which keeps this below the "Established" threshold despite OMIM assignment of a disease entity. Strong supporting biology (mitoribosome assembly, mtDNA transcription/translation roles of MRPL12 with POLRMT) reinforces plausibility, so a residual share goes to Hypothesized; "Novel" is essentially excluded.

Atrial standstill 2 (OMIM 615745) is attributed to biallelic NPPA mutation based primarily on a single consanguineous Italian family (Disertori/Quintarelli et al., Circ Cardiovasc Genet 2013) in which a homozygous NPPA truncating/frameshift variant segregated with atrial dilated cardiomyopathy progressing to atrial standstill, with heterozygous carriers largely unaffected. This is credible human genetic evidence but, to my knowledge, has not been robustly replicated in independent probands, which argues for "Existing" rather than "Established." Supporting context comes from heterozygous NPPA frameshift variants causing familial atrial fibrillation (Hodgson-Zingman, NEJM 2008), a closely related atrial myopathy/arrhythmia phenotype, and from functional/animal data showing mutant ANP with altered cardiac/atrial electrophysiology. Some probability remains for "Established" because the gene–disease pair is curated in OMIM/gene panels and additional families may have been reported.

The strongest human genetic evidence is a single multigenerational family in which a SIRT1 missense mutation (L107P) co-segregated with autoimmune type 1 diabetes, with functional support showing increased nitric oxide/inflammatory signaling in beta cells and lymphocytes (Biason-Lauber et al., Cell Metab 2013). Additional candidate-gene/polymorphism studies have reported associations of SIRT1 variants or altered SIRT1 expression with other autoimmune conditions (SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, IBD, thyroid autoimmunity), but these are small, inconsistently replicated, and often expression- rather than variant-based. Because replication across independent probands or families is lacking, "Established" is not warranted, while the single credible family study plus supportive association reports justify most weight on "Existing." Substantial mechanistic biology — SIRT1 deacetylation of RORγt and FOXP3 modulating Th17/Treg balance, NF-κB regulation, and amelioration/worsening of murine lupus, EAE and colitis by SIRT1 modulation — supports a meaningful "Hypothesized" allocation. "Novel" is essentially excluded given the volume of mechanistically relevant immunology literature.

STT3B encodes one of the two catalytic subunits of the oligosaccharyltransferase complex, and biallelic STT3B variants were reported in a patient with a congenital disorder of glycosylation (STT3B-CDG, CDG-Ix; OMIM 615597) in the same study that defined STT3A-CDG, with supporting biochemical demonstration of hypoglycosylation in patient fibroblasts and rescue by wild-type cDNA. The mechanism is directly relevant since loss of STT3B impairs post-translocational N-glycosylation of skipped sequons. However, unlike STT3A-CDG, human reports for STT3B remain extremely limited (essentially one or very few probands), so replication across independent families is weak, which is why the evidence is credible but not firmly established. Most of the probability therefore falls on "Existing," with a substantial minority on "Established" given the strong functional validation and OMIM/ClinGen-level recognition of the disease entity.

The main human genetic evidence linking TNK2 (ACK1) to epilepsy comes from a single consanguineous family in which a homozygous missense variant segregated with severe autosomal recessive infantile-onset epilepsy (Hitomi et al., Ann Neurol 2013), supported by in vitro functional data showing altered ACK1 autophosphorylation. This is a single family with an early-onset, encephalopathy-like phenotype rather than classic genetic generalized epilepsy, and the association has not been robustly replicated; TNK2 is not among the loci identified in large GGE GWAS (ILAE Consortium 2014/2018/2023) or in major GGE exome/panel studies. Therefore evidence for TNK2 in GGE specifically is limited and arguably indirect, warranting mostly "Existing" with substantial weight on "Hypothesized" (biological plausibility via CDC42/ACK1 signaling in neuronal development and synaptic function) and some weight on "Novel" because the reported phenotype is not GGE and the gene–disease relationship has been questioned/limited in curation efforts.

Congenital generalized hypertrichosis terminalis with or without gingival hyperplasia (CGHT, OMIM 135400) was first mapped to copy-number variants at 17q24.2-q24.3, a region containing/flanking ABCA5, in several unrelated probands (Sun et al., AJHG 2009). A subsequent study identified a homozygous ABCA5 missense variant in a consanguineous family with congenital generalized hypertrichosis plus gingival hyperplasia, supported by functional work implicating lysosomal cholesterol transport and ABCA5 expression in hair follicles (DeStefano et al., 2014). However, the CNVs are large and may act through position effects rather than ABCA5 coding disruption, and independent replication of pathogenic ABCA5 point mutations is sparse, so the causal role is suggestive rather than definitive. This places the evidence mostly in the "Existing" category with some probability of "Established," and residual weight on purely biological/functional support.

ADCY1 was proposed as the gene underlying the DFNB44 locus (7p14.1–q11.22) based on a homozygous missense variant segregating in a consanguineous Pakistani family with nonsyndromic recessive hearing loss, supported by zebrafish knockdown showing hair cell and hearing defects (Santos-Cortez et al., Hum Mol Genet 2014). This constitutes credible human genetic evidence from a single family, with the mechanistic support coming largely from animal/in vitro work (cAMP signaling in hair cells), so the evidence is not replicated across multiple independent probands. ClinGen Hearing Loss expert curation has, to my knowledge, rated ADCY1 at the "Limited" level, consistent with an "Existing" rather than "Established" classification. A smaller share of points is assigned to Hypothesized to reflect that much of the supporting functional evidence is non-human, and minimal weight to Novel given the existence of at least one human family report.

BMP signaling is central to calvarial osteogenesis and suture patency, and human genetic evidence firmly implicates this pathway in isolated (nonsyndromic) craniosynostosis — notably the BMP2 risk locus from GWAS of sagittal and metopic synostosis and loss-of-function variants in the BMP antagonist SMAD6. For BMP7 specifically, however, I am not aware of replicated human studies showing causal or associated variants in isolated craniosynostosis; mentions arise mainly from candidate-gene/exome screens without convincing statistical or segregation support, and occasionally from contiguous 20q13 deletions with variable craniofacial findings. The strongest BMP7-specific evidence is biological: expression in developing cranial sutures/osteogenic fronts, potent osteoinductive activity, and murine Bmp pathway perturbations producing craniofacial and suture phenotypes. Therefore most weight falls on Hypothesized, with a modest allocation to Existing for possible isolated human variant reports within BMP-pathway sequencing studies, and a small residual to Novel.

DNAH8 encodes an axonemal outer dynein arm heavy chain and was proposed in early genomic work (ca. 2000) as a positional/functional candidate gene for primary ciliary dyskinesia, but systematic mutation screening of PCD cohorts has not confirmed it as a PCD gene. The robust human genetic evidence for DNAH8 instead links bi-allelic loss-of-function variants to multiple morphological abnormalities of the sperm flagella (MMAF) and asthenoteratozoospermic male infertility, with reported patients explicitly lacking respiratory/situs manifestations of PCD; DNAH8 expression appears largely testis-enriched. Because sperm flagellar dysmotility from an outer dynein arm defect is a recognized component/mechanism shared with PCD, some weight belongs in "Existing," but the absence of replicated PCD-affected probands keeps "Established" very low. The strongest support is for a biologically plausible, mechanism-based relationship ("Hypothesized"), with a residual possibility that the gene is effectively unrelated to classical PCD.

FBXO32 (atrogin-1/MAFbx) was reported as a dilated cardiomyopathy gene in a consanguineous family by Al-Yacoub et al. (Genome Biology, 2016), where a homozygous missense variant segregated with early-onset DCM and was supported by functional work showing impaired SCF-complex/ubiquitin-ligase activity; follow-up functional studies implicated ER-stress-mediated apoptosis. However, replication in independent probands/families has been minimal, and expert gene-curation efforts (e.g., ClinGen DCM panel) have generally placed FBXO32 in a limited-evidence tier rather than definitive, so "Established" receives few points. Substantial supporting biology exists independently of human genetics: atrogin-1 regulates calcineurin-dependent hypertrophic signaling and cardiac autophagy, and mouse knockouts develop cardiomyopathy, which underpins the Hypothesized allocation. Because at least one credible human genetic report exists, "Novel" is essentially excluded.

IARS2 encodes the mitochondrial isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase; biallelic variants are firmly established as causing CAGSSS syndrome (cataracts, growth hormone deficiency, sensory neuropathy, sensorineural hearing loss, skeletal dysplasia) and a broader spectrum of mitochondrial disease. Several case reports describe patients with biallelic IARS2 variants presenting with Leigh or Leigh-like syndrome, including Japanese siblings reported by Takezawa et al. with overlapping CAGSSS/Leigh/West syndrome features, plus additional isolated cases in mitochondrial disease cohorts. Mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase defects are a well-recognized mechanistic class causing Leigh syndrome, which strengthens biological plausibility. However, the number of independent Leigh-phenotype probands remains relatively small and the core IARS2 phenotype in most reports is CAGSSS rather than classic Leigh syndrome, so the evidence is credible but not yet definitive/replicated at the level of an established gene–disease pair.

phenotype: complex neurodevelopmental disorder with or without congenital anomalies
justification: KIF4A is an X-linked kinesin gene reported in human neurodevelopmental disease: Willemsen et al. (2014) described a family with a Xq13.1 deletion/disruption of KIF4A segregating with intellectual disability, plus additional missense variants, with functional work showing effects on synaptic function. Subsequent X-exome/large ID cohort studies and scattered case reports have added hemizygous KIF4A variants in males with ID, epilepsy, and occasional congenital anomalies, but the total number of independently reported, well-segregated probands remains small, and OMIM lists the association provisionally (MRX100, "?"). This pattern is typical of a "Limited/Moderate" gene–disease validity classification rather than definitive, so Existing receives the bulk of points, with some probability that curators considered the replication sufficient for Established. Supporting mouse/in vitro data on KIF4A in neuronal survival, chromosome segregation, and synaptic function provide the biological plausibility underlying the Hypothesized remainder; outright Novel is very unlikely given the published human genetic reports.

KPNA7 (importin alpha 8) was implicated in a human neurodevelopmental disorder by Puffenberger et al. (2012), who identified a homozygous missense variant (p.Glu344Gln) segregating in Old Order Amish siblings with severe developmental delay, dysmorphism and epilepsy/seizures, discovered via homozygosity mapping and exome sequencing. A small number of additional case reports and functional studies (impaired nuclear import/cargo binding, altered localization of mutant KPNA7 in cell models) support pathogenicity, but independent clinical replication remains limited, so the gene–epilepsy link is credible yet not firmly established. Epilepsy in these patients is part of a broader syndromic neurodevelopmental phenotype rather than isolated epilepsy. Functional/cell-biology and zebrafish work adds mechanistic plausibility, justifying some weight on Hypothesized, while the existence of at least one human genetic report makes Novel very unlikely.

RGS6 is best characterized in humans for associations with heart rate/sinoatrial function, cancer susceptibility, and substance-use/alcohol-related phenotypes rather than classic neurodevelopmental disease. Its neurobiology is highly relevant, however: RGS6 is strongly expressed in cerebellum, striatum and hippocampus, and Rgs6-knockout mice show dopaminergic neuron loss, ataxia-like and anxiety/depression-like behavioral phenotypes, giving a solid "Hypothesized" basis. I also have a partial recollection of recent reports (≈2022–2024) of biallelic loss-of-function RGS6 variants in consanguineous families with developmental delay/intellectual disability, hyperkinetic movement disorder and cerebellar atrophy, which, if confirmed and replicated across independent families, would push the evidence toward Existing/Established; because I cannot confidently verify these reports, I keep most weight on Existing and Hypothesized. A small residual probability is assigned to Novel in case all human NDD links are incidental co-mentions.

RPS20 entered the hereditary colorectal cancer literature through Nieminen et al. (2014, Gastroenterology), who used linkage and exome sequencing in a large Finnish family fulfilling Amsterdam criteria for HNPCC but without mismatch-repair deficiency, identifying a segregating germline missense variant (p.Val54Leu) with supporting functional data on ribosome biogenesis. Subsequent reports (e.g., Danish and other familial/early-onset CRC cohorts) have described additional rare RPS20 variants, but replication is sparse and validation studies such as Broderick et al. have questioned the evidence for several recently proposed CRC predisposition genes. Importantly, the associated phenotype is MMR-proficient familial colorectal cancer ("Lynch-like"/familial CRC type X) rather than classical Lynch syndrome, which is defined by MLH1/MSH2/MSH6/PMS2/EPCAM defects. This yields credible but limited human genetic evidence for a closely related/overlapping phenotype, supporting "Existing" rather than "Established," with residual weight on "Hypothesized" given the largely functional/ribosomopathy mechanistic support.

phenotype: epilepsy, early-onset, with or without developmental delay
justification: SETD1A loss-of-function and de novo missense variants have been reported in human cohorts with early-onset epilepsy and neurodevelopmental impairment, forming the basis of the OMIM entry "Epilepsy, early-onset, with or without developmental delay" (MIM 618832). The key report (Yu et al., Neuroscience Bulletin 2019) described de novo and inherited SETD1A variants in Chinese children with early-onset epilepsy, and additional support comes from large epilepsy/neurodevelopmental exome studies (Epi4K/EuroEPINOMICS, DDD) and from the SETD1A haploinsufficiency syndrome series (Kummeling et al. 2021), in which seizures occur in a subset of patients. Replication across independent probands is reasonable but the epilepsy-specific phenotype is less firmly delineated than the broader neurodevelopmental/schizophrenia association, so some weight remains on "Existing." Supporting biology (SETD1A as an H3K4 methyltransferase, Drosophila and mouse models with neuronal/behavioral phenotypes) is consistent but is not the primary evidence base.

phenotype: congenital anomaly of kidney and urinary tract
justification: SIX2 encodes the master transcription factor of the cap mesenchyme nephron progenitor population, and Six2-null mice show premature progenitor depletion with severe renal hypoplasia/dysplasia, providing very strong biological plausibility. In humans, Weber et al. (2008, JASN) reported rare heterozygous SIX2 variants (including a frameshift) with functional impairment in patients with renal hypodysplasia, and SIX2 has since been included in many CAKUT gene panels and cohort resequencing studies. However, replication in independent large CAKUT cohorts has been sparse, variants are often rare missense of uncertain significance, and gene-disease validity curation generally regards the evidence as limited rather than definitive. Therefore the bulk of probability falls on "Existing," with a meaningful share for "Established" (given panel inclusion and additional case reports) and for "Hypothesized" (reflecting that much of the strongest evidence is murine/functional).

phenotype: sacral agenesis-abnormal ossification of the vertebral bodies-persistent notochordal canal syndrome
justification: This specific syndrome (OMIM 615709, "sacral agenesis with vertebral anomalies") was defined by Postma et al. (J Med Genet 2014), who identified a homozygous TBXT (T/brachyury) missense variant segregating with the phenotype in a consanguineous family with multiple affected individuals, supported by functional assays showing reduced transcriptional activity. The gene–disease link is therefore human-genetic and disease-defining, but replication in independent, unrelated probands is sparse, so the evidence is credible yet not firmly replicated — consistent with a "Limited/Moderate" ClinGen-style classification. Strong supporting biology exists from Brachyury mouse mutants with sacral/caudal agenesis and notochord defects, and TBXT variants have been linked to human neural tube defects and chordoma, reinforcing notochord-related pathogenicity. I therefore place most weight on Existing with substantial weight on Established.

Biallelic TSEN54 variants (notably the recurrent p.Ala307Ser founder allele) are a well-replicated cause of pontocerebellar hypoplasia types 2A, 4 and 5, confirmed in many independent probands and families across multiple cohorts. These disorders are defined by cerebellar hypoplasia/atrophy with progressive cerebellar signs; surviving milder patients have been described with ataxia, dysarthria and cerebellar atrophy, and some reports describe TSEN54-related phenotypes within the spectrum of early-onset/congenital cerebellar ataxia. Because "cerebellar ataxia" is a phenotype closely tied to, though not identical with, the canonical PCH presentation (which is dominated by severe dyskinesia, spasticity and profound developmental impairment), I place most weight on Established with substantial residual weight on Existing. Functional and animal/in vitro data on tRNA splicing endonuclease complex dysfunction support the mechanism but are not the primary evidence base.

APC2 is the gene listed in OMIM for autosomal recessive intellectual developmental disorder 74, based initially on a consanguineous family with a homozygous loss-of-function APC2 variant producing Sotos-like features and intellectual disability (Almuriekhi et al., Cell Reports 2015). Subsequent reports have described additional families with biallelic APC2 variants causing a neurodevelopmental phenotype with intellectual disability and cortical malformations (e.g., polymicrogyria-like gyral anomalies), supporting replication, though the total number of independent probands remains relatively modest. Strong supportive biology exists from Apc2-null mice, which show cortical lamination defects, abnormal axonal projections, and learning impairment, consistent with a causal mechanism. I therefore split points mostly between Established and Existing, reflecting that the human genetic evidence is credible and at least partly replicated but not as extensive as for classic ID genes.

ASPN is the gene assigned to OMIM "osteoarthritis susceptibility 3" based on Kizawa et al. (2005, Nature Genetics), who reported that the aspartic acid (D14) repeat allele of asporin is over-represented in Japanese knee and hip OA patients and functionally inhibits TGF-β–mediated chondrogenesis. Replication has been obtained in additional Asian cohorts (Han Chinese, Korean) and in some meta-analyses, supporting a real but population-restricted association. However, several well-powered European/Caucasian studies (UK, Spanish, Greek) failed to replicate the D14 association, so the causal role is not definitively established across populations. Supportive functional data (asporin binding TGF-β1, suppressing aggrecan/COL2A1 expression, cartilage expression gradients) and related associations with lumbar disc degeneration strengthen biological plausibility. Hence most weight goes to "Existing," with substantial but not dominant weight to "Established."

Biallelic CLPB variants are firmly established as causing 3-methylglutaconic aciduria type VII (MEGCANN) with cataracts, neurologic involvement (hyperekplexia, seizures, encephalopathy) and neutropenia, and heterozygous dominant-negative variants cause severe congenital neutropenia; these are human genetic findings but the neuroimaging phenotype is typically brain atrophy, white matter abnormalities, and corpus callosum anomalies rather than the symmetrical basal ganglia/brainstem necrotizing lesions that define Leigh syndrome. CLPB is a mitochondrial intermembrane-space AAA+ disaggregase, so it is biologically plausible to be included in mitochondrial encephalopathy/Leigh-spectrum differential diagnoses and panels, which supports a hypothesized link. I am not aware of a well-documented, replicated series of CLPB patients with radiologically and clinically confirmed Leigh syndrome, so Established receives minimal weight. A small amount of weight goes to Existing because isolated Leigh-like descriptions in mitochondrial disease cohorts or panel-based studies may exist, and because CLPB deficiency is a recognized mitochondrial encephalopathy. The remaining weight reflects genuine uncertainty that the specific Leigh phenotype has ever been credibly attributed to CLPB.

HNRNPA0 is not among the genes implicated in Tourette syndrome by the main human genetic studies, which have highlighted SLITRK1, HDC, CELSR3, WWC1, NIPBL, FN1, CNTN6, NRXN1, and the FLT3 locus from GWAS. I am not aware of any replicated or even single credible human genetic study linking HNRNPA0 variants to Tourette syndrome or to a recognized TS precursor/subtype. As a broadly expressed hnRNP involved in mRNA stability and p38/MK2 signaling, it is conceivable that it could appear in a brain-expression or network/pathway analysis of neurodevelopmental disorders, which leaves a small amount of weight for a hypothesized biological link. Overall, the evidence profile is best described as novel, with modest residual probability that an exome/CNV or pathway paper has mentioned it incidentally.

Waardenburg syndrome type 2F (OMIM 619947) is specifically attributed to heterozygous variants in KITLG, based principally on the report by Zazo Seco et al. (AJHG 2015), which described allelic KITLG mutations causing both asymmetric/unilateral hearing loss and WS2 in more than one family, with functional support. KITLG/KIT signaling is central to melanocyte migration and survival, and mouse Steel (Kitl) mutants show white spotting and deafness, providing strong biological plausibility consistent with the WS2 phenotype. Subsequent sporadic reports and cohort screening of WS patients have added some, though limited, replication, and the number of independent probands remains modest compared with MITF or SOX10. I therefore weight Established most heavily but retain substantial probability on Existing because the human genetic evidence rests largely on a single landmark study plus scattered case reports.

phenotype: early-childhood-onset neurodegeneration with retinitis pigmentosa, sensorineural hearing loss, and demyelinating peripheral neuropathy
justification: KLC4 encodes kinesin light chain 4, a kinesin-1 adaptor whose biology (long-range axonal/intraflagellar-type cargo transport, photoreceptor and sensory neuron maintenance) is directly relevant to a neurodegenerative syndrome combining retinitis pigmentosa, sensorineural hearing loss and demyelinating neuropathy; paralog KLC2 causes SPOAN syndrome, strengthening the biological rationale. The best-documented human genetic evidence for KLC4 is a homozygous variant in a consanguineous Turkish family with complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia (Bayrakli et al., 2015), which is a related but not identical neurodegenerative phenotype. I have some recollection of more recent reports/curations describing biallelic KLC4 variants in a childhood-onset neurodegeneration syndrome with retinal dystrophy, hearing loss and demyelinating neuropathy, but I cannot confirm multiple independent, replicated families, so "Established" receives few points. Supporting functional work exists mainly in zebrafish klc4 mutants (axon branching/sensory axon defects), which supports "Hypothesized" rather than human causal evidence. Because the phenotype description is unusually specific and likely derives from at least one published human proband/family, I weight "Existing" highest while retaining some probability that the association is essentially unreported.

NDUFV2 encodes the 24 kDa flavoprotein subunit of mitochondrial complex I, and biallelic pathogenic variants are an accepted cause of mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 7 (MC1DN7), in humans. The best-documented cases (e.g., the IVS2+5G>A splice variant reported by Bénit and colleagues) presented with early-onset hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and encephalopathy, and subsequent patients have been described with Leigh/Leigh-like neuroradiological features; NDUFV2 appears in curated gene lists for Leigh syndrome. However, the number of independent probands with a formal Leigh syndrome diagnosis is small compared with better-established complex I genes such as NDUFV1, NDUFS1–S8, so the evidence for the specific Leigh phenotype is credible but not as extensively replicated. Strong mechanistic support (complex I assembly/activity defects, nuclear-encoded complex I deficiency being the commonest cause of Leigh syndrome) underpins the biological plausibility. Points are therefore split mainly between Established and Existing, with a minority on Hypothesized.

PRICKLE1 is the gene for autosomal-recessive progressive myoclonus epilepsy–ataxia syndrome (EPM1B, OMIM 612437), based on a homozygous missense variant (R104Q) segregating in consanguineous families of Middle Eastern origin reported by Bassuk et al. (2008), with supporting functional and Drosophila/mouse data. A follow-up study (Tao et al., 2011) identified additional heterozygous PRICKLE1 (and PRICKLE2) missense variants in patients with myoclonic epilepsy and showed seizure phenotypes in prickle-deficient flies and mice, strengthening but not definitively proving dominant contributions. Independent replication beyond these related groups is comparatively limited, and some gene-curation efforts have considered the evidence moderate rather than overwhelming, so I retain substantial weight on "Existing." Animal and interaction/expression data (planar cell polarity, synapsin I interaction) provide the mechanistic basis supporting a small residual "Hypothesized" allocation.

PRIMA1 encodes the proline-rich membrane anchor that tethers acetylcholinesterase at synapses, placing it directly in the cholinergic pathway implicated in sleep-related/nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy (CHRNA4, CHRNB2, CHRNA2). A single human report (Hildebrand et al., Ann Clin Transl Neurol 2015) described a homozygous PRIMA1 deletion in two siblings from a consanguineous family with nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy and intellectual disability, supported by functional data showing loss of membrane-anchored AChE and by Prima1-null mouse data. This constitutes credible but non-replicated human genetic evidence from one family, so "Existing" is most appropriate; replication in independent probands is lacking, limiting "Established." Supporting biology (AChE anchoring, cholinergic synaptic transmission, knockout mouse phenotypes) justifies residual weight on "Hypothesized." Little basis exists for "Novel."

There is a specific human genetic report implicating PRIMA1 in nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy: Hildebrand and colleagues (2015) described a homozygous ~50 kb deletion removing PRIMA1 in two affected siblings from a consanguineous-like family with nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy, proposing autosomal recessive inheritance. This is a single family without independent replication in additional probands, so the evidence falls short of "Established." The biological rationale is strong and complementary: PRIMA1 anchors acetylcholinesterase at synaptic membranes, and disruption of cholinergic signalling is the established mechanism in ADNFLE caused by CHRNA4, CHRNB2 and CHRNA2 mutations; Prima1-null mice show altered cholinergic transmission, which supports but does not by itself establish causation in humans. Accordingly, most weight goes to "Existing," with residual weight on "Hypothesized" (animal/functional data) and a small amount on "Established."

SPP2 (secreted phosphoprotein 2 / SPP24) is primarily known from bone/BMP-binding biology, but I recall at least one human genetic report (around 2019, from a Chinese cohort) proposing heterozygous SPP2 variants as a cause of autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa, supported by segregation in one or a few families plus supporting expression/functional work in retina and animal models. This evidence has not, to my knowledge, been widely replicated in independent cohorts, and SPP2 is not among the well-validated, routinely screened adRP genes, so it falls short of "Established." The biological plausibility (retinal expression, secreted protein affecting photoreceptor/RPE homeostasis, animal model data) would independently justify "Hypothesized" if the human genetic claim is discounted. I therefore place most weight on Existing, with meaningful residual probability on Hypothesized and a small chance that the association is spurious/nonexistent.

TNNI1 encodes slow skeletal troponin I, a core thin-filament regulatory protein in the same complex as TNNT1 and TPM3/TPM2, which are well-established childhood-onset nemaline myopathy genes, so the biological rationale for involvement is strong (supporting Hypothesized). However, TNNI1 is not part of the standard, replicated nemaline myopathy gene panel list (ACTA1, NEB, TPM2, TPM3, TNNT1, CFL2, KBTBD13, KLHL40, KLHL41, LMOD3, MYPN, MYO18B, TNNT3), and I am not aware of multiple independent probands with rod-containing myopathy attributed to TNNI1. I recall reports linking TNNI1 variants to human skeletal muscle phenotypes in the congenital contracture/distal arthrogryposis–congenital myopathy spectrum, which would be a related but not identical phenotype; such reports justify some weight on Existing. Because my recollection of any specific human nemaline-myopathy case with TNNI1 is uncertain, I keep Established low and retain some probability on Novel.

USP27X was proposed as a novel X-linked intellectual disability gene in the large X-exome sequencing study of unresolved XLID families by Hu et al. (2016, Molecular Psychiatry), which reported a truncating/loss-of-function variant segregating with non-syndromic ID, and it is catalogued in OMIM as X-linked intellectual developmental disorder (MRX105) and in curated ID gene lists (SysID). However, the number of independently reported probands/families remains small, with limited published replication and mostly segregation plus deubiquitinase-pathway plausibility (USP27X stabilizes MYC/SNAIL and is a paralog of the ID-associated USP9X/USP7 family) rather than robust functional proof in patient-derived systems.
